newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia cuts list of 'war criminals' in Serb enclave.
newsitem.headline: Croatia cuts list of 'war criminals' in Serb enclave.

text.p: Croatia has drafted a new list of 175 wanted Serb war criminals, a fraction of the previously mentioned number, presumed living in a breakaway enclave due to return to government rule soon, officials said on Thursday.
President Franjo Tudjman handed the list on February 17 to Jacques Klein, the U.S. diplomat serving as administrator of the U.N. mission in the area known as Eastern Slavonia.
"As far as we are concerned, we consider this to be the final list," a government spokeswoman told Reuters.

Eastern Slavonia is due to "reintegrate" into Croatia soon after April elections in a peaceful end to an ethnic conflict that started in 1991 when minority Serbs opposing Croatia's independence from Yugoslavia carved out their own mini-state.
The process is being enforced by 5,000 United Nations troops who last year dissolved Serb rebel forces in the enclave, estimated to be inhabited by 120,000 Serbs.

A previous list of more than 800 Serb war crimes suspects did little to allay fears among Serb men and their families in Eastern Slavonia that they would face persecution and random arrest once Croatian refugees and police returned.
A U.N. official in the enclave told Reuters by telephone the list of names was still being discussed but "this (one) could well become the final one".

Envoys from the U.N. mission had pressed Tudjman's government for months to issue a more precise and reliable list to help persuade Serbs not to flee the enclave en masse before reintegration is complete in the early summer.

Croatia has already amnestied all Serbs who took part in the 1991 rebellion except those accused of war atrocities. But Tudjman's government took a while to draft a definitive list of the Serbs it wanted to see in court.

Croatian government troops recaptured two other breakaway Serb enclaves in 1995 and more than 150,000 Serbs fled before or after the assault to Serb-held Bosnia and Yugoslavia, with which Zagreb established diplomatic ties last year.

The state-run newspaper Slobodna Dalmacija said on Thursday the new list was headed by Goran Hadzic, a former separatist leader of Eastern Slavonia Serbs who sank into obscurity after plans for the area's peaceful reintegration gained momentum,
"Now all the Serbs except those on the list can remain to live in (the enclave) without fear of prosecution, on the condition they accept the Croatian state," the daily said.

It said the list included former Yugoslav Army General Mile Mrksic, believed to be now living in Serbia across the Danube River border from Eastern Slavonia, and the current mayor of the enclave's main town Vukovar, Miroslav Keravica.

Vukovar, a Danube port once graced by neo-classical architecture from the Austro-Hungarian era, was reduced to rubble by the Yugoslav army and local Serb militia in a bloody three-month siege that ended in November 1991.
There was no official Serb reaction to the new list.

U.S. Ambassador Peter Galbraith, who visited Eastern Slavonia on Wednesday, was quoted as telling the Serbs that Croatia would have to stick to its pledges on human and minority rigts or risk being ostracised by the West.
